Scent brings the lover into the poem

The opening joins a name with the smell of fine oils. The comparison makes attraction felt through the senses. Wine, scent, and touch belong to the poem’s language of desire. Read these images as poetic comparisons, not a list of objects owned by the lovers. Ancient perfume vessels help make that sensory world concrete.

The return of flowers and birds accompanies the lover’s call to come outside. Nature gives desire a shared rhythm and setting. The repeated warning about awakening love places timing beside the invitation.

The night scene turns longing into movement through streets and questions to guards. Finding the beloved changes absence into physical closeness. The later royal procession widens the poem’s scale without explaining every connection between its scenes.
The garden describes desire through a place

An enclosed garden joins beauty with protected access. The following lines name fruit, spices, and flowing water. These images describe the beloved through abundance and invitation. They do not give a route to a garden we can locate. Notice how the woman’s response develops the image rather than merely receiving it.
A missed opening changes the scene

The beloved’s departure turns an expected meeting into searching. The guards now injure the woman instead of merely receiving her questions. Her later praise preserves desire while the encounter remains unresolved.
Belonging follows a question about absence
Other voices ask where the beloved has gone. The woman answers through garden imagery and mutual belonging. The scene gives her knowledge and speech a central role in restoring the relation.
Praise leads into the woman’s invitation

Descriptions of the body fill much of the chapter. The woman then proposes travel and meeting among growing plants. Her voice gives desire its own direction rather than only receiving another speaker’s praise.
The ending places love beyond purchase

The poem measures love against floodwaters and wealth. The comparisons give desire a force money cannot command. This claim follows scenes of searching, meeting, and separation. Read it as the collection’s final statement about love’s value. A gift of wealth cannot replace the relation the speakers seek.
